class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Setup data from storyboard
        title_text = "The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels"
        lecture_lines = [
            "We calculate the average weight of squirrel groups.",
            "Each sample mean becomes a single data point.",
            "Repeating this process creates a new data distribution."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Colors from storyboard
        GREY_COLOR = "#808080"
        BLUE_COLOR = "#0000FF"
        
        # Static elements: Axis at the bottom (Row F)
        axis = Line(self.grid["F1"], self.grid["F6"], color=WHITE)
        axis_label = Text("Sample Mean Weight", font_size=16, color=WHITE).next_to(axis, DOWN, buff=0.2)
        self.add(axis, axis_label)

        # Assets
        squirrel_svg_path = "/mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/squirrel.svg"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Color line 1 to match elements (Grey/White context)
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(GREY_COLOR))
        
        # 10 squirrels representing individual squirrels (Asset Integration)
        squirrel_template = SVGMobject(squirrel_svg_path, color=GREY_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.8).scale(0.3)
        squirrels = VGroup(*[squirrel_template.copy() for _ in range(10)])
        squirrels.arrange_in_grid(rows=2, cols=5, buff=0.2)
        
        # Positioning according to Issue 40 fix
        self.place_in_area(squirrels, "C2", "D5", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(squirrels))
        self.wait(0.5)
        
        # Calculate average and display number above a blue dot
        avg_val = 502
        avg_label = Text(f"{avg_val}g", font_size=20, color=WHITE)
        sample_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.1)
        
        # Positioning according to Issue 41 fix
        self.place_at_grid(sample_dot, 'E3', scale_factor=0.8)
        avg_label.next_to(sample_dot, UP, buff=0.2)
        
        self.play(
            Write(avg_label),
            FadeIn(sample_dot)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Color line 2 to match elements (Blue)
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE_COLOR))
        
        # The blue dot falls vertically onto the axis
        # Position it on the axis (Row F)
        target_x = sample_dot.get_x()
        target_y = self.grid["F3"][1] + 0.1
        
        self.play(
            sample_dot.animate.move_to([target_x, target_y, 0]),
            FadeOut(avg_label),
            FadeOut(squirrels),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Color line 3 to match elements (Blue)
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(BLUE_COLOR))
        
        # Stacking logic setup
        bin_counts = {}
        bin_width = 0.4
        dot_radius = 0.08
        
        def get_stack_pos(x_val):
            # Map x_val to a bin index based on the axis range
            # Range F1 to F6 is roughly from x=0.5 to x=5.5
            start_x = self.grid["F1"][0]
            bin_idx = int((x_val - start_x) / bin_width)
            count = bin_counts.get(bin_idx, 0)
            bin_counts[bin_idx] = count + 1
            # Stack dots upwards from the axis
            return np.array([start_x + bin_idx * bin_width + bin_width/2, self.grid["F1"][1] + 0.1 + count * (dot_radius * 1.5), 0])

        # Register the first dot in the bins
        first_bin_idx = int((target_x - self.grid["F1"][0]) / bin_width)
        bin_counts[first_bin_idx] = 1

        # Repeat the process a few times with visual squirrel flashes
        for _ in range(5):
            # Flash squirrel group (Issue 42 fix)
            temp_sq = VGroup(*[squirrel_template.copy() for _ in range(10)])
            temp_sq.arrange_in_grid(rows=2, cols=5, buff=0.1)
            self.place_in_area(temp_sq, "C2", "D5", scale_factor=0.6)
            
            # Generate a new sample mean dot
            # Sample around the center of the axis
            center_x = (self.grid["F1"][0] + self.grid["F6"][0]) / 2
            rand_x = center_x + random.uniform(-1.5, 1.5)
            new_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=dot_radius)
            # Start from the squirrel group area (Row C/D)
            new_dot.move_to([rand_x, self.grid["D3"][1], 0])
            
            self.play(
                FadeIn(temp_sq, run_time=0.2),
                FadeIn(new_dot, run_time=0.2)
            )
            
            # Dot falls and stacks
            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)
            self.play(
                new_dot.animate.move_to(stack_pos),
                FadeOut(temp_sq, run_time=0.2),
                run_time=0.6
            )

        # Speed up the process (Rapidly stacking dots)
        fast_dots_animations = []
        num_fast_dots = 60
        for i in range(num_fast_dots):
            # Sampling from a normal distribution for visual effect (CLT demo)
            # The underlying squirrel weights are uniform, but sample means are normal
            center_x = (self.grid["F1"][0] + self.grid["F6"][0]) / 2
            rand_x = random.gauss(center_x, 0.7)
            # Clamp to axis bounds
            rand_x = max(self.grid["F1"][0] + 0.2, min(self.grid["F6"][0] - 0.2, rand_x))
            
            fast_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=dot_radius * 0.7)
            # Start falling from above (Row B)
            start_pos = np.array([rand_x, self.grid["B3"][1], 0])
            fast_dot.move_to(start_pos)
            
            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)
            
            # Use a slight delay for each dot
            delay = i * 0.04
            # We add the dots to the scene but they are initially invisible or moved in Succession
            anim = Succession(
                Wait(delay),
                FadeIn(fast_dot, run_time=0.1),
                fast_dot.animate.move_to(stack_pos).set_run_time(0.2)
            )
            fast_dots_animations.append(anim)

        # Render the rapid sampling
        self.play(AnimationGroup(*fast_dots_animations))
        self.wait(3)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Initialize layout
        self.setup_layout("The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell", [
            "- Watch as sample means begin to pile up.",
            "- A symmetric bell shape naturally starts to form.",
            "- This is the birth of the Normal Distribution."
        ])
        
        # Define hex colors
        BLUE_HEX = "#0000FF"
        WHITE_HEX = "#FFFFFF"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Lecture: "- Watch as sample means begin to pile up."
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE_HEX))
        
        # Create an axis for the histogram
        axis = Line(self.grid["E1"], self.grid["E6"], color=WHITE)
        axis_label = Text("Sample Means", font_size=20, color=WHITE)
        # Fix for Issue 44: Center label below axis using area F3-F4
        self.place_in_area(axis_label, "F3", "F4", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Create histogram bars
        num_bars = 12
        bar_width = 0.35
        bars = VGroup()
        
        # Start bars at zero height
        for i in range(num_bars):
            bar = Rectangle(
                width=bar_width,
                height=0.01,
                fill_color=BLUE_HEX,
                fill_opacity=0.7,
                stroke_width=1,
                stroke_color=BLUE_HEX
            )
            # Distribute bars across columns 1 to 6 on row E
            x_pos = self.grid["E1"][0] + i * (self.grid["E6"][0] - self.grid["E1"][0]) / (num_bars - 1)
            bar.move_to([x_pos, self.grid["E1"][1], 0], aligned_edge=DOWN)
            bars.add(bar)
        
        self.add(axis, axis_label, bars)
        
        # Initial jagged piling animation
        jagged_heights = [0.2, 0.8, 1.5, 0.4, 2.2, 1.1, 2.5, 0.9, 1.8, 0.5, 1.2, 0.3]
        self.play(
            *[bars[i].animate.stretch_to_fit_height(jagged_heights[i], about_edge=DOWN) for i in range(num_bars)],
            run_time=2.0
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Lecture: "- A symmetric bell shape naturally starts to form."
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE_HEX))
        
        # Symmetric heights for bars (Gaussian-like)
        def gaussian(x, mu, sig):
            return 3.5 * np.exp(-np.power(x - mu, 2.) / (2 * np.power(sig, 2.)))
        
        smooth_heights = [gaussian(i, (num_bars-1)/2, 2.0) for i in range(num_bars)]
        
        self.play(
            *[bars[i].animate.stretch_to_fit_height(smooth_heights[i], about_edge=DOWN) for i in range(num_bars)],
            run_time=2.0
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Lecture: "- This is the birth of the Normal Distribution."
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE_HEX))
        
        # Define the bell curve shape
        bell_curve = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: 3.5 * np.exp(-0.5 * (x / 1.0)**2),
            x_range=[-3, 3],
            color=WHITE_HEX,
            stroke_width=4

outline.topic: The Magic of the Central Limit Theorem: Order from Chaos
outline.target_audience: Introductory Statistics Students / Undergraduate University Students

sections.title: Introduction: The Hidden Pattern
sections.content: Start with a visual of a chaotic, 'ugly' distribution (e.g., a bimodal or skewed histogram). Introduce the mystery: no matter how weird the starting population looks, if we group them together, a perfect 'Bell Curve' emerges. Explain that this is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).
sections.example: Imagine a forest where animal weights are completely random—some tiny beetles, some massive elephants, and nothing in between. The graph looks like a mess.

sections.title: Prerequisite Checklist: Population vs. Sample
sections.content: Briefly define the 'Population' (everyone) and its Mean (μ). Contrast this with a 'Sample' (a small group) and its Mean (x̄). Use a magnifying glass graphic to show picking a small group out of the large crowd.
sections.example: Population: All 1,000 squirrels in the park. Sample: A random group of 30 squirrels we caught and weighed today.

sections.title: The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels
sections.content: Introduce the process of repeated sampling. We take a sample of size 'n', calculate the mean, and plot it on a new graph. Then we do it again. And again. Visualize a 'Mean-o-Matic' machine that takes groups of squirrels and spits out a single average weight dot.
sections.example: Robot 'Sample-Bot' picks 10 random squirrels, averages their weight to 500g, and drops a blue marble on a scale. It repeats this 1,000 times.

sections.title: The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell
sections.content: Show an animation where the 'Sample Means' histogram starts to pile up. Even if the original squirrel weights were skewed, the pile of blue marbles starts to form a symmetric Normal Distribution shape. Highlight the key concept: The distribution of sample means is always Normal if the sample size is large enough.
sections.example: As 'n' (the number of squirrels in each group) increases from 2 to 30, the jagged graph of dots magically smooths out into a perfect, glowing Bell Curve.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Sample Size (n ≥ 30)
sections.content: Introduce the mathematical 'Magic Number' 30. Explain that for most distributions, once your sample size reaches 30, the CLT 'kicks in' and the normal approximation becomes reliable. Use a 'Power Meter' visual that turns green when n reaches 30.
sections.example: If 'Sample-Bot' only picks 2 squirrels, the graph is still messy. When it picks 30 squirrels per group, the Bell Curve becomes undeniable.

sections.title: The Math: Mean and Standard Error
sections.content: Introduce the formulas graphically. The center of the new Bell Curve is the same as the original population mean (μ). However, the Bell Curve is narrower. Show the formula for Standard Error: σ / √n. Visually demonstrate that as 'n' gets bigger, the Bell Curve gets taller and skinnier (more precise).
sections.example: Show a wide, flat bell curve for n=30 and a very thin, sharp needle-like bell curve for n=1000, representing higher certainty.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Quality Control
sections.content: Explain why this matters. Since we know the shape of sample means is a Bell Curve, we can predict probabilities even if we don't know the full population distribution. This is used in everything from medical trials to manufacturing.
sections.example: A candy factory bot measures the average sugar in 50 bars. Even if some bars are slightly off, CLT tells the manager the probability that the *average* of the batch is within safety limits.

sections.title: Summary: The Bridge to Statistics
sections.content: Recap: 1. Start with any distribution. 2. Take large samples (n ≥ 30). 3. The means will be Normally distributed. Conclude that the CLT is the bridge that allows us to use Normal Distribution math on almost anything in the universe.
sections.example: Final visual: A bridge made of Bell Curves connecting a chaotic world of data to a structured world of scientific prediction.

improvements.problem: The chaos_text label ('CHAOS') is a single word but spans the entire width of the top row (A1-A6) at default scale, making it appear disproportionately large and dominant.
The histogram area (B1-E6) lacks internal padding, causing the tallest bars to nearly touch the 'CHAOS' text above, creating vertical congestion.
The clt_text ('Central Limit Theorem') is a long label positioned at the extreme bottom edge of the grid (F1-F6), which risks appearing cramped or slightly cut off depending on resolution.
The 'pop_label' at A3 is positioned too high, causing it to crowd the title and clip against the top edge of the frame.
The 'sample_label' at F4 is scaled too large in the final scene, causing it to touch the bottom boundary and risk being cut off.
The 'pop_label' persists after the transition to the sample focus, creating a messy overlap with the enlarged green sample circle.
improvements.solution: Add self.play(FadeOut(pop_label)) before the scaling animation at the final lecture line (approx. line 105).

formula_mean is positioned at point A3, which is too high and causes vertical imbalance on the right side of the screen.
formula_se at C3 is too close to the top formula, leaving the bottom half of the grid (rows D-F) entirely empty and unused.
The top grid row (A1-A6) is currently unused, causing the overall layout to appear bottom-heavy and underutilizing available space.
